I just don't understand the science behind it. If you drink a glass of water after eating peanut butter, you still have peanut butter stuck in your teeth, but if you drink a glass of milk, the peanut butter is blissfully wisked away. Why is that?
How is it that milk can just neutralize peanut butter in your mouth?
Oils in the milk that coat your mouth is my guess.
Milk is an emulsion, it's quite good at dissolving certain types of oils and fats. Water generally isn't.

Peanut butter is mostly made of peanut solids and peanut oil. Because peanut oil is hydrophobic, when you try to wash away the peanut butter in your mouth the oils repel the water and end up passing right by it. Milk, while being mostly water, has fats suspended in it. Fats and oils are essentially the same thing. When you drink milk, these fats can dissolve into the peanut oil more easily. I'm guessing that milk fat is less hydrophobic than peanut oil, and allow the mixture of peanut oil and milk fat to dissolve into the milk more easily.
